messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: I want to compute the mean and covariance of a matrix
parts:
Hi, I want to compute the mean and covariance of a matrix. My current code is kinda ugly. Does Stan have a function to do this? Or is there cleaner code anyone can recommend? No big deal but this is going into a paper that people might read, so I might as well do it right! My code is below (it’s part of the transformed parameters block, and it computes the mean M_tilde and the cov matrix Sigma_tilde of the J_tilde*T_tilde matrix a_tilde). I’m pretty sure I can replace that last line with crossprod(), but I’d like to get rid of the loop too, if possible. Writing as a function is another option, but can a Stan function return a list of 2 outputs?
A


for (t in 1:T_prime){
M_tilde[t] <- mean(row(y_tilde, t));
for (j in 1:J_tilde)
y_tilde_centered[j,t] <- y_tilde[j,t] - M_tilde[t];
}
Sigma_tilde <- y_tilde_centered'*y_tilde_centered/(J_tilde-1);
Sigma_tilde <- .5*(Sigma_tilde + Sigma_tilde');

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: I want to compute the mean and covariance of a matrix
parts:
On Friday, April 10, 2015 at 2:00:23 PM UTC-4, Andrew Gelman wrote:
Hi, I want to compute the mean and covariance of a matrix.  My current code is kinda ugly.  Does Stan have a function to do this?
Not for the covariance matrix.
Or is there cleaner code anyone can recommend?
(crossprod(matrix) - N * tcrossprod(mean_vector)) / (N - 1);
Writing as a function is another option, but can a Stan function return a list of 2 outputs?

Only if the two outputs have homogenous types and the same sizes. That is not the case for a mean vector and a covariance matrix.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: I want to compute the mean and covariance of a matrix
parts:
On Friday, April 10, 2015 at 6:07:10 PM UTC-4, Andrew Gelman wrote:
I’ll have to think about it.  In teaching statistics we always define var as E((y-E(y))^2), never E(y^2) - (E(y))^2.  We do so both for stability and conceptual reasons.  I can’t imagine that subtracting first is actually costing much if anything in autodiffing.  That is, I’d prefer crossprod(matrix - mean_vector(matrix))).

I am a fan of the principle to never compute something the way it is defined in textbooks (although all the textbooks derive as a theorem E[yy'] - E[y]E[y]'), but the cost depends on how big the number of rows there are relative to the number of columns. If you sweep the mean vector from all the columns that is N * K subtractions before doing the crossprod() and if you do the crossprod first, it is K * K subtractions, K * K multiplications by N, and K + K choose 2 multiplications to obtain tcrossprod(mean_vector).

Ben

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: I want to compute the mean and covariance of a matrix
parts:
What Ben says! Using

E[y^2] - E[y]^2

The point is never ever do subtractions when you don't have
to because you can lose arbitrary amounts of precision when the
numbers are close to each other. For example, if the numbers
are close to each other, as in

1.1111 - 1.1110 = .0001

you go from five digits of precision down to 1.
You also have underflow issues, so that

1 - 1e-16 == 1

So you lose either the amount of shared prefix if they're close
or the difference if they're far away. Subtraction is just bad news
for floating point numbers.

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] I want to compute the mean and covariance of a matrix
parts:
Maybe I'm misunderstanding who's saying what, so let me
start from first principles.

Calculating as

E[y^2] - E[y]^2 = 1/N SUM_n y[n]^2 - (1/N SUM_n y[n])^2

only involves a single subtraction and that subtraction
has to be done, whereas

E[(y - E[y])^2] = 1/N SUM_n (y - E[y])^2

involves N subtractions.

For scalars, of course, you can just use var(y). It's for vectors
that we don't have something built in and for that we should have a covar()
function built in with custom gradients that implements the result and
gradients stably so users don't have to worry about it.

- Bob

P.S. I think arithmetic stability of Stan code is a reasonable user-facing
issue, but feel free to move to stan-dev if you'd prefer.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] I want to compute the mean and covariance of a matrix
parts:
Bob, I have to disagree here. The problem with
E[y^2] - E[y]^2 is that you’re subtracting two big
numbers, while E[(y - E[y])^2] subtracts two smaller
numbers and hence have higher floating point
precision. E[(y - E[y])^2] is almost always recommended
but it’s slow as it requires two passed through the data.
Welford accumulators compute E[(y - E[y])^2] in a
single pass using clever analytic manipulations.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] I want to compute the mean and covariance of a matrix
parts: It's not the size of the numbers, it's the ratio

> On Apr 11, 2015, at 7:48 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Bob, I have to disagree here. The problem with
> E[y^2] - E[y]^2 is that you’re subtracting two big
> numbers, while E[(y - E[y])^2] subtracts two smaller
> numbers and hence have higher floating point
> precision.

Subtraction of (x - y) is problematic when either:

* x/y is close to 1

* x >> y or y >> x

The size of the numbers doesn't matter at all, at least until
you overflow or underflow what a double can represent and
that's not going to happen until some y[n] > 1e100 or y[n] < 1e-100
and then some.

Now we know that E[y^2] >= E[y]^2 in general and we have
to somehow represent that difference, because it's the final
result, so it seems that computing both terms themselves
then subtracting them is more stable than the other way around.

Unless of course, E[y^2] overflows but no (y[n] - E[y])^2
overflows.

Am I missing something critical here?

> E[(y - E[y])^2] is almost always recommended
> but it’s slow as it requires two passed through the data.
> Welford accumulators compute E[(y - E[y])^2] in a
> single pass using clever analytic manipulations.

I agree that the Welford approach is the way to go --- I've
been saying that since long before I worked on Stan!

- Bob

>>>>> I’ll have to think about it. In teaching statistics we always define var as E((y-E(y))^2), never E(y^2) - (E(y))^2. We do so both for stability and conceptual reasons. I can’t imagine that subtracting first is actually costing much if anything in autodiffing. That is, I’d prefer crossprod(matrix - mean_vector(matrix))).
>>>>>
>>>>> I am a fan of the principle to never compute something the way it is defined in textbooks (although all the textbooks derive as a theorem E[yy'] - E[y]E[y]'), but the cost depends on how big the number of rows there are relative to the number of columns. If you sweep the mean vector from all the columns that is N * K subtractions before doing the crossprod() and if you do the crossprod first, it is K * K subtractions, K * K multiplications by N, and K + K choose 2 multiplications to obtain tcrossprod(mean_vector).
>>>>>
>>>>> Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] I want to compute the mean and covariance of a matrix
parts:
Just for clarity here, the page recommends Welford's algorithm or
an ad-hoc approximation thereof to avoid catastrophic cancellation,
and also clearly states you shouldn't use E[(y - E[y])^2] directly
in practice, either.

I don't believe our existing functions are particularly
stable, either. Here's a feature request if anybody wants to
take it on:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/1423

It should be a relatively easy, yet important and non-trivial project
to get started working on Stan if someone's looking for a point of
entry.

- Bob

> On Apr 12, 2015, at 3:28 AM, Aki Vehtari <aki.v...@aalto.fi> wrote:
>
> https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algorithms_for_calculating_variance

> provides reasons why
> E[y^2] - E[y]^2
> should not be used in practice.
>
> Page also includes analysis of other approaches.
>
> Aki
>
> On Saturday, April 11, 2015 at 7:32:58 PM UTC+3, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> It's not the size of the numbers, it's the ratio
> > On Apr 11, 2015, at 7:48 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Bob, I have to disagree here. The problem with
> > E[y^2] - E[y]^2 is that you’re subtracting two big
> > numbers, while E[(y - E[y])^2] subtracts two smaller
> > numbers and hence have higher floating point
> > precision.
>
> Subtraction of (x - y) is problematic when either:
>
> * x/y is close to 1
>
> * x >> y or y >> x
>
> The size of the numbers doesn't matter at all, at least until
> you overflow or underflow what a double can represent and
> that's not going to happen until some y[n] > 1e100 or y[n] < 1e-100
> and then some.
>
> Now we know that E[y^2] >= E[y]^2 in general and we have
> to somehow represent that difference, because it's the final
> result, so it seems that computing both terms themselves
> then subtracting them is more stable than the other way around.
>
> Unless of course, E[y^2] overflows but no (y[n] - E[y])^2
> overflows.
>
> Am I missing something critical here?
>
> > E[(y - E[y])^2] is almost always recommended
> > but it’s slow as it requires two passed through the data.
> > Welford accumulators compute E[(y - E[y])^2] in a
> > single pass using clever analytic manipulations.
>
> I agree that the Welford approach is the way to go --- I've
> been saying that since long before I worked on Stan!
>
> - Bob
